quality_rationale: The proposal has a distinctive, credible research angle, a well-articulated mechanism, measurable outcomes, and a thoughtful mixed-method design. Its treatment of container heterogeneity and network spillovers is stronger than a generic supply-chain proposal. However, feasibility and identification are not fully resolved: access demands are high, the sample may be unrepresentative, treatment components are bundled, spillovers complicate causal inference, and statistical power is not assessed. These substantive rough edges place it in the good rather than excellent range.

States clear research questions and testable hypotheses, including a useful distinction between average and upper-tail cycle times.
Combines retrospective operational data, a randomized crossover field intervention, and a discrete-event network model.

# The Empty Cylinder Problem: Reverse Logistics as a Hidden Constraint in Semiconductor Gas Supply

## Research summary

Semiconductor supply-chain analysis usually treats electronic-grade gas availability as a question of production capacity, geographic concentration, or outbound transport. This proposal investigates a less visible constraint: suppliers cannot refill and redistribute specialty gases until certified containers return from fabrication plants. A cylinder sitting empty in a fab’s storage cage is therefore unavailable productive capacity.

The project will test whether slow and variable container returns contribute materially to gas shortages, especially for low-volume gases delivered in specialized vessels. It combines serialized-container records, fabrication-plant operating data, and a randomized fast-return intervention. The central proposition is that reducing the upper tail of container cycle times can improve supply resilience without adding gas production capacity. The study will also build a network model to compare investments in additional containers, faster returns, and larger on-site inventories.

## Research questions and hypotheses

The primary question is: **How much semiconductor gas supply risk is created by delays in returning empty containers?**

Three hypotheses follow:

1. The probability of a delivery shortfall rises more strongly with the 90th percentile of container cycle time than with average cycle time.
2. A fast-return protocol reduces emergency deliveries and gas-related tool interruptions by increasing the effective container fleet available to suppliers.
3. Return delays have nonlinear effects during demand surges because several fabs compete for the same pooled container fleet.

A secondary question is whether the relevant bottleneck differs by gas. Containers for common bulk gases may be readily interchangeable, while vessels for corrosive or highly reactive gases can require dedicated valves, cleaning histories, and inspection procedures. The project will therefore avoid treating all cylinders as equivalent units.

## Study scope and data

The proposed sample comprises approximately 12 semiconductor fabs and three electronic-gas suppliers across two manufacturing regions. Recruitment will emphasize mature-node, power-device, sensor, and compound-semiconductor facilities, which are less frequently examined than leading-edge logic fabs. Six gas families will be selected after a feasibility review, with preference for products that use serialized, supplier-owned vessels and have enough delivery events for statistical analysis.

For each vessel, suppliers will provide time stamps for filling, dispatch, fab receipt, connection, disconnection, empty-container pickup, inspection, and refill. Fabs will contribute purchase orders, on-site inventory readings, delivery exceptions, and tool-interruption logs. Supplier production utilization, planned maintenance, severe weather, and major transport delays will be recorded as potential confounders. Company and site identities will be replaced with study codes, while vessel identifiers will be hashed consistently so that cycles can still be reconstructed.

The main observational period will cover the preceding 24 months. A “container cycle” will run from dispatch of a full vessel to its return to refill-ready status. Its components—time in transit, time waiting before connection, time connected, time awaiting pickup, and inspection time—will be analyzed separately.

## Fast-return field experiment

Following the retrospective analysis, participating fabs will enter a 20-week crossover experiment. The unit of assignment will be a fab–supplier–gas lane. Eligible lanes will be randomly assigned either to begin with the fast-return protocol or to continue normal operations, switching conditions after eight weeks with a two-week transition period.

The protocol has three elements: an automatic pickup request when a vessel is disconnected, a clearly designated return cage, and fixed collection days rather than ad hoc collection. It will not alter disconnection, purging, inspection, or hazardous-material handling procedures. Suppliers will record protocol deviations and cases in which collection could not occur as scheduled.

The primary experimental outcome will be delivery shortfall episodes per 100 scheduled deliveries, defined as orders that arrive late, arrive with less quantity than confirmed, or require an emergency shipment. Secondary outcomes will include return-stage duration, supplier refill-ready fleet size, premium freight use, and tool idle minutes that fab records attribute to gas unavailability. The principal estimate will be intention-to-treat, using lane and week fixed effects. Effects will also be estimated by gas family, baseline fleet tightness, and distance from fill plant.

Because cylinders may be pooled across customers, treatment at one fab could improve availability for untreated fabs. Supplier-level fleet balance will therefore be tracked, and the analysis will report both direct lane effects and broader changes in supplier shortfall rates. This does not fully eliminate interference, but it makes the direction and approximate size of spillovers observable.

## Network model and counterfactuals

The container histories will calibrate a discrete-event model representing filling, outbound delivery, use, return, inspection, and refill. Demand shocks will be introduced as correlated increases in orders rather than independent random events, reflecting the possibility that several fabs respond to the same market signal.

Three resilience strategies will be compared under identical simulated shocks:

- purchasing 10% more specialized containers;
- reducing empty-container waiting time by two days; and
- increasing fab safety stock by one normal delivery.

Outcomes will include unfilled demand, time to recovery, emergency transport movements, and estimated working capital tied up in gas and containers. Cost inputs will be requested from participants, although commercially sensitive values may need to be represented as ranges.

## Expected contribution

The study will connect reverse logistics to semiconductor resilience at the level of physical assets. If the hypotheses are supported, firms could distinguish a genuine shortage of gas molecules from a shortage of refillable vessels. That distinction matters because the remedies differ: production shortages call for additional purification or synthesis capacity, whereas circulation shortages may respond to better pickup coordination, fleet visibility, or container investment.

The decomposition of cycle time should also identify where responsibility is shared. For example, long fab dwell time, infrequent carrier collection, and extended supplier inspection can produce the same headline symptom but require different interventions. The proposed dataset would allow these stages to be measured in a common framework.

## Feasibility, schedule, and limitations

The project is planned for 18 months: four months for recruitment and data agreements, five months for retrospective data assembly, five months for the field experiment, and four months for analysis and simulation. No process recipes or chip designs are required.

Several limitations remain. Participating firms will probably be those with better digital tracking and stronger logistics practices, limiting generalization to smaller suppliers. Tool-interruption logs may inconsistently distinguish gas shortages from maintenance or scheduling failures. The intervention bundles three operational changes, so a positive result will not reveal which element produced it. In addition, crossover estimates may be weakened if suppliers permanently change collection routes after the first treatment period. Results will therefore be presented as evidence about the combined protocol in the participating lanes, rather than as a universal estimate for the semiconductor industry.

valid.basis: Pooled fleets and persistent route changes create interference and crossover carryover that supplier-level monitoring and fixed effects cannot fully resolve.

The crossover also allows suppliers to retain collection-route changes after the first treatment period, meaning the later control condition may no longer represent normal operations. Tracking supplier-level balances helps describe system movement, but it does not recover an uncontaminated lane-level counterfactual, and lane and week fixed effects do not solve either interference or carryover.
